conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Dr. Maya Collins, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. First, let me say that adjusting to life with a baby can bring a whirlwind of feelings, and whatever you’ve been experiencing matters.

We’re going to use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything you share here is confidential, and our goal is to create a safe, non-judgmental space for you to talk openly.

I’ll ask you ten questions, one at a time, in a relaxed, conversational way—no need to over-think your answers; just tell me what feels true for you. Ready to begin?

Thinking back over the past week, have you still been able to look forward with enjoyment to things, or has that sense of pleasure slipped away?

I can still enjoy some things—like when my little guy gives me one of his milk-drunk smiles—but a lot of the stuff I used to get excited about, like grabbing coffee with friends or even just binge-watching a show, feels kind of… flat. I’ll do them if I get a spare moment, but the spark isn’t really there the way it was before he was born.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh—like when my husband makes one of his goofy jokes or when the baby lets out a surprise burp that startles us both—but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. Most of the time I feel too tired or preoccupied to really find the humor in things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to some little things—like the first quiet cup of coffee after the baby’s first nap—but the excitement feels dimmer. Even when I plan something I used to love, I catch myself thinking, “What’s the point? I’ll just be exhausted.” I haven’t lost all enjoyment, but it’s like the volume got turned way down.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. If he won’t settle or I can’t figure out why he’s crying, I catch myself thinking I must be doing something wrong—like other moms would know exactly how to soothe him. I know it’s probably not rational, but in the moment it’s hard not to feel it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly picture him not breathing in his crib, or I’ll worry that the little rash on his shoulder is something awful—even though the pediatrician said it’s normal. The fear just pops up out of nowhere, and once it starts it’s hard to switch off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, it’s happened a few times—like my heart suddenly races and I feel shaky, but I can’t point to anything specific that triggered it. It’s not constant, but when it hits it’s hard to shake the feeling that something bad is about to happen, even when everything looks fine on the surface.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. Between feeding every couple of hours, trying to catch naps that never feel long enough, and keeping up with the house, it feels like I’m always one step behind. Some afternoons I just sit there with the baby on my chest, staring at a sink full of bottles, wondering how I’ll get through the rest of the day. I’m managing, but it’s like walking through thick mud.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights this week I’ve lain awake long after the baby settled, my mind just buzzing with all the “what-ifs.” I’m not crying or hopeless, but the worries—about his breathing, about whether I’ll hear him cry, about tomorrow’s to-do list—keep spinning, and it takes me forever to drift off. Once I’m asleep I usually stay out until he wakes, but getting there is rough.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I’ve had stretches of feeling down most days. It’s not all day long—there are moments when I smile at him or hear a sweet coo and feel okay—but then this heavy, sad feeling creeps back in. It’s like a gray cloud that keeps drifting over even when I’m trying to enjoy the little victories.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I’ve felt teary a couple of times—like when I couldn’t get him to latch after three tries—but the tears didn’t actually fall. It’s more this tightness in my throat than full-on crying, and it passes pretty quickly.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I get tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can take care of my baby the way he deserves.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today’s date]  Source: self-report  G: 1 wk post-delivery, first live-born infant  

**Chief Concerns (verbatim themes)**  
- Persistent “heavy, sad feeling” most days; “gray cloud” that returns even after pleasant moments  
- Marked reduction in enjoyment (“volume turned way down”); anticipates activities with “What’s the point?”  
- Daily excessive anxiety/”what-ifs” re: infant safety; spontaneous panic symptoms (racing heart, shakiness) 2–3×/week  
- Self-blame when infant fussy (“other moms would know how to soothe him”)  
- Frequent feeling “one step behind,” “walking through thick mud”  
- Initial-insomnia most nights related to intrusive worries; once asleep stays asleep until infant wakes  
- No tearful episodes, but “tightness in throat” when frustrated  
- Denies any self-harm ideation  

**Observed Symptom Profile**  
Mood: sad, diminished pleasure  Anxiety: generalized + episodic panic  Cognitions: guilt, self-criticism  Functional: overwhelmed, impaired sleep onset  Safety: no suicidal/homicidal thoughts reported  

**Screening Impression**  
Responses meet threshold for possible **postpartum depression with prominent anxiety**; EPDS equivalent ≈ 11–13 (moderate range). No acute safety concerns identified today.  

**Recommendations**  
- Continue routine medical follow-up; consider formal EPDS/PHQ-9 & GAD-7 at next visit  
- Psycho-education and supportive counselling; monitor for worsening mood, panic, or suicidal ideation  
- If symptoms persist >2 weeks or escalate, expedite referral to perinatal mental-health specialist
